e-218.problem:
Each side of a square is decreasing at a rate of $2\,\text{cm/min}.$ How fast is the area of the square decreasing when the sides are $10\,\text{cm}?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095797/assets/a06eb0963dc6d01e45acb9349e5232ba70a11c98c99ee63c2ec0dae3d748f5ed.png)
e-218.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} .
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A = x^2.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is decreasing at a rate of $2\,\text{cm/min},$ so we have $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} = -2.$ Also, when the sides are $10\,\text{cm},$ we have $x=10.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =(-2)\cdot 2(10)=-40{\text{ cm}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square decreases at a rate of $40\,\text{cm}^2/\text{min}.$

e-219.problem: The area of a square decreases at a rate of $20 \text{ cm}^2\text{/s}.$ If $x$ and $A$ denote the side length and area of the square respectively, then find an expression for $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds.
e-219.worked_solution:
This situation is different. Here, the *area* is changing at a constant rate,  and we want to know the rate at which the side lengths are changing.

First, let's draw a diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095797/assets/f4125cebd7553bb8b106a8baff39a6e4a120b9d9e5cdf2c4c9c0a9a676558897.png)

We want to find $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}.$ The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A = x^2.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We know from the given information that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-20\text{ cm[math]^2[/math]/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this information, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}-20 & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{10}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

e-221.knowledge_point: Relating the Rate of Change of a Diagonal Length to Another Rate of Change
e-221.problem: The sides of a square are increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the square is numerically equal to twice the rate of increase of the diagonal. What is the area of the square at that moment?
e-221.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the area of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A = \dfrac{h^2}{2}.
$$

Using implicit differentiation and the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

The given information tells us that $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = 2\dfrac{\textrm d h}{\textrm d t}$, so replacing $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm dt}$ in the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =h\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ 2\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} & =h\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} \\ 2 & =h.\end{aligned}
$$

So at that particular moment, we have $h=2,$ and therefore the area of the square at that moment is

$$
A = \dfrac{2^2}{2} = 2.
$$

In a testing facility, a scientist is increasing the diagonals of a simple square at a rate of $12 \text{ mm}\text{/min}.$ At what rate, in squared millimeters per minute, is the area of the square increasing when the length of the diagonal is $6\, \text{mm}?$
e-220.worked_solution:
Let $h$ and $A$ be the length of the diagonals and the area of the square, respectively. Using the Pythagorean theorem, it can be shown that the relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A = \dfrac{h^2}{2}.
$$

We want to find

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $h$ increases at a rate of $12\,\textrm{mm/min},$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we want to compute the rate of change of the area when the diagonal has length $h=6.$ Substituting this information into our expression for $\dfrac{\textrm{d}A}{\textrm d t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =12\cdot 6=72{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is decreasing at a rate of $5\,\text{m/s},$ so we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-5.$ Also, when the sides are $1\,\text{m},$ we have $x=1.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =(-5)\cdot 2(1)=-10{\text{ m}}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square decreases at $10\,{\text{m}}^{2}/\text{s}.$

content.problem: The area of a square increases at a rate of $4{\text{ m}}^{2}\text{/s}.$ At what rate are the lengths of the sides of the square increasing when the sides are $1\text{ m}$ long?
content.worked_solution:
Here, the area is changing at a constant rate,  and we want to know the rate at which the side lengths are changing.

First, let's draw a diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095797/assets/e920b14f0a8c3e16c4108da5b252721c7751b7ae978b8d4740445c7087c169c6.png)

We want to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We know from the given information that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =4\text{ m}{}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this information, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when the sides are $1\,\text{m},$ we have $x=1.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{1}=2.
$$

Therefore, the lengths of the sides are increasing at a rate of $2\,\text{m/s}.$

The sides (in feet) of a square are increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the square is numerically equal to four times the rate of increase of the diagonals. What is the length of the diagonals of the square at that moment?

a
12.5 feet
b
8 feet
c
5.5 feet
d
4 feet
e
6 feet
Submit

decision.explanation: Let h be the length of each diagonal. Since A=h²/2, dA/dt=h(dh/dt). The given relation is dA/dt=4(dh/dt); canceling the positive diagonal growth rate gives h=4 feet.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: The sides (in feet) of a square are increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the square is numerically equal to four times the rate of increase of the diagonals. What is the length of the diagonals of the square at that moment?
after.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the area of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

The given information tells us that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=4\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$, so replacing $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ in the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =h\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ 4\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} & =h\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} \\ 4 & =h.\end{aligned}
$$

So at that particular moment, we have that the length of the diagonals of the square is $4\text{ feet}.$

4dhdt=hdhdt4dhdt=hdhdt4=h.

Let $p$ be the perimeter of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $p$ and $h$ is

$$
p=2\sqrt{2}h.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(p) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(2\sqrt{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each diagonal of the square is decreasing at a rate of $3\sqrt{2}\text{ m}\text{/min},$ so we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=-3\sqrt{2}.
$$

Substituting this information into the above expression for $\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =(-3\sqrt{2})\cdot (2\sqrt{2})=-12\text{ m/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the perimeter of the square decreases at $12\text{ m}/\text{min}.$

A graphic designer is reducing the diagonals of a simple square on the screen at a rate of 2.5 mm/s. At what rate, in squared millimeters per second, is the area of the square decreasing when the length of the diagonal is 12.4mm?

a
 18 mm2/s
b
 25 mm2/s
c
37 mm2/s
d
31 mm2/s
e
 29 mm2/s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let h and A be the length of the diagonals and the area of the square, respectively. Using the Pythagorean theorem, it can be shown that the relationship between A and h is

A=h22.

We want to find

dAdt.

Differentiating this relationship with respect to t using implicit differentiation, we get

ddt(A)=ddt(h22)dAdt=dhdt⋅ddh(h22)dAdt=dhdt⋅h.

We're told that h decreases at a rate of 2.5mm/s, so

dhdt=−2.5.

Also, we want to compute the rate of change of the area when the diagonal has length h=12.4. Substituting this information into our expression for dAdt, we get

dAdt=−2.5⋅12.4=−31 mm2/s.

We conclude that the area of the square is decreasing at a rate of 31 mm2/s.

A graphic designer is reducing the diagonals of a simple square on the screen at a rate of $2.5\text{ mm}\text{/s}.$ At what rate, in squared millimeters per second, is the area of the square decreasing when the length of the diagonal is $12.4\,\text{mm}?$
content.worked_solution:
Let $h$ and $A$ be the length of the diagonals and the area of the square, respectively. Using the Pythagorean theorem, it can be shown that the relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $h$ decreases at a rate of $2.5\,\text{mm/s},$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we want to compute the rate of change of the area when the diagonal has length $h=12.4.$ Substituting this information into our expression for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-2.5\cdot 12.4=-31{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the area of the square is decreasing at a rate of $31{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$
